    Engine · paper only

    The Paper League

    Seventeen autonomous $100,000 paper books — the fifteen graders, the Skeptic and The Bot — filled at the first open after the board sits, held to the close five sessions on, marked at 18:00 and ranked on a live leaderboard, with a clean SPY-hedged column beside the booked equity. A scoreboard, not a record of skill. Paper only, by construction.

    What the League is#

    Every seat that grades gets a book. The Paper League (bablytics/paper.py) runs seventeen fully autonomous paper accounts — the fifteen grading members, the Skeptic, and The Bot 🤖, which mechanically trades the Executive's signed book — each starting at $100,000 (the paper_start_equity setting). It is a self-scoring simulation with no real money and no connection to the broker: the League exists so the leaderboard can show which philosophies actually made money on paper, and so every member's daily convictions leave a priced trail the reviews can grade.

    The roster is derived, never listed: it is GRADING_MEMBERS + [skeptic, bot], so seating a new grader grows the League by one book with no code change and no edit to this page. It is seventeen books today because there are fifteen graders; older docs quote smaller numbers because there were fewer seats when they were written.

    The rules, exactly#

    The rules are deterministic and documented in the module's docstring; nothing here is discretionary.

    How a book opens#

    Once a morning run completes, the pipeline calls open_positions_for_run once (it is idempotent per run — if the run already has paper rows, nothing happens):

    1. Graders and the Skeptic each take up to three leads on which they took a non-neutral stance, ranked by conviction |grade − 50| descending (ties broken by the lead's rank). Direction follows the stance: bull → long, bear → short.
    2. The Bot takes the first five leads of the book's printed rank order, whatever the grade, direction exactly as the lead was ranked (long or short). The rank is the # on each lead card: one order across the share and option columns, not a standing within one column. A lead with no rank sorts after every ranked one, then by final grade, then by ticker. Changed 2026-10-07, from the first book opened after the ruling: until then the Bot took the top five by final grade with final grade ≥ 60 (why it changed).
    3. One leg per ticker per book. A run's leads can carry the same underlying twice — two theses, one name. The best-placed lead claims the ticker and the freed slot passes to the next distinct name, so a seat never doubles a position by agreeing with both. A unique index on (member, run, ticker) enforces the same rule in the database, so a doubled leg cannot be written even by a bug.
    4. Size = 10 % of the member's current equity ÷ entry price — "current equity" being the latest equity snapshot dated strictly before the run date, or the start equity for a seat with no history. Fractional shares are allowed down to 0.0001. All of a member's same-day picks size off that one basis.
    5. Entry price. It depends on when the book is written (round 59, 2026-09-28).
      • Before 09:30 ET: the entry is that day's open. The rows wait pending until the open prints, then are priced on the next mark with the same sizing basis.
      • At or after 09:30 ET, which is most days, because the board usually sits after the open: the entry is the next session's open, held four sessions, so the exit is still the close of the run bar plus five. Until then a book booked at the day's open was credited with the open-to-freeze move its seats had already watched. That credit flattered the seats that buy what has already moved (Sam, Herald, Flow) and cost the contrarian ones (Black Swan, Graham, Timekeeper).
      Existing rows are not rewritten. From the entry session the Bailiff and the Midday Check-In price a pending row first, so a trigger can exit it. On the run date itself the book is still waiting for the next open, and the Last action column reads pending: opens X at the <date> open.

    Every leg is shares of the lead's ticker. An option lead is traded as its underlying — the League does not price contracts.

    The doubled-book correction (2026-09-08). The one-leg-per-ticker rule was added after the fact. The runs of 2026-08-18 and 2026-08-19 each listed a ticker in two leads, and pick selection then had no such rule — eleven legs across nine books were opened twice, and because each snapshot walks the whole ledger, every equity number from 18 August on was computed over the doubled rows. The surplus legs were removed (keeping the first-written leg of each pair — the one the midday desk had been closing first anyway), every snapshot from 2026-08-18 was re-marked from the corrected ledger, and the Pyramid's money basis was refreshed. All nine books gained, because every doubled leg was a loser: watchdog +$1,107 and dagger +$1,098 at the far end, four books around +$212 at the near end. The crown did not move.

    Marking and closing#

    mark_to_market runs from the 18:00 outcomes job, right after realized outcomes are recorded, and on demand. For each member, in order: price any pending entries whose open bar now exists; close any priced position held for five trading days — the exit bar is the entry bar's index plus five in the ticker's own daily series, closed at that bar's close once its date has arrived (a missing bar falls back to the last known close); then recompute the member's equity from scratch off the whole position ledger and upsert one snapshot for the day (paper_equity is unique per member and date, so re-marking a day is idempotent and never drifts). Weekends and holidays fall out naturally because prices come from daily bars.

    The cash arithmetic, including shorts. Starting from cash = start equity: a long open spends cash (qty × entry); a short open credits the proceeds. On close a long sale credits cash; a short cover spends it. Anything still open is marked at the current price — a long as an asset, a short as a liability to buy back. Equity = cash + open value. Worked in the module: long 10 shares @ 100 → mark 110 → close 120 gives 100,000 → 100,100 → 100,200; short 10 @ 100 → 90 → cover 80 gives the same +200. Both round trips are commented in the code so the accounting can be checked by hand.

    Why a leg closes#

    exit_kindWho closed itWhenReason recorded
    (null)the calendarthe fifth trading day after entry, at the closenone — the scheduled hold expired
    middaythe member, at the 12:30 Midday Check-Inat the midday markthe member's own sentence ("stop paying vig", "harvest convexity")
    bailiffthe Bailiff, only when enforcement is switched onwhen a written ruling fires on its basisthe board's written condition, verbatim

    A day in the League#

    • after the board

      Books open#

      The morning run finishes and every seat's picks are written pending. A book written before 09:30 ET enters at that day's open. One written after the open, which is the usual case, enters at the next session's open.

    • 12:30 ET

      Midday Check-In#

      All fifteen graders and the Skeptic read their own open paper positions marked at midday and file one hold-or-close per position. Closes are applied immediately with the member's reason; the League page shows them in a Midday adjustments card (headline, board tilt, the closes-applied feed, per-member reads). The Bot does not attend — it follows the Executive's book mechanically.

    • during the session

      The Bailiff (if enforcing)#

      A fired ruling closes every member's leg in that ticker for the run, tagged bailiff. Off by default; see dry run versus enforce.

    • 18:00 ET

      Mark to market#

      Pending entries are priced at the open, five-day holds are closed at the close, and every seat's equity snapshot for the day is recomputed from the ledger.

    Windows, win rate and the table#

    The table sorts by highest balance by default, and every meaningful column is sortable — click a heading to sort by it, click again to reverse. Blank cells always sink to the bottom whichever way the arrow points, so a seat with no win rate cannot top the table by having no data. The crown is computed from equity independently of the sort: it marks the biggest book, and it stays on that seat when you sort by name or win rate instead of wandering to whoever happens to be in the top row.

    The leaderboard shows each seat's equity and its P&L over a selectable window — 1D · 1W · 1M · YTD · 6M. The server computes window P&L by comparing the latest equity snapshot with the last snapshot on or before a cutoff: 1, 7 and 30 calendar days back, 182 days for 6M, and the prior year's last snapshot for YTD; where the seat has no snapshot that old the cell is empty rather than invented. Win rate counts closed trades only. The table's other columns are open-position count, a Last action line in words ("closed NEM midday — stop paying vig", "opened HL 2026-08-14"; on the same day a close outranks an open), and Trend — an inline SVG equity sparkline drawn from /api/paper/league/history, no chart library. The leader wears a crown; The Bot is highlighted as the benchmark; the footnote states the start equity.

    Clean, hedged: the same picks, measured without the League's conventions#

    The leaderboard's equity is as booked: entered at the open, sized at 10% of compounding equity, and closed early by the Midday Check-In, which accounts for 42% of all closes. Beside it the table prints two columns (round 59):

    • Clean, hedged re-prices each seat's own picks on one fixed basis: entry at the next session's open, exit at the close of the run bar plus five, $10,000 a position with no compounding, midday exits ignored, and the four historical mock runs (1, 2, 29, 33) excluded. It then subtracts what the S&P 500 did over the same window in the same direction. It shows whether the picks beat the market, not whether the book grew. Positions that cannot be priced are counted and flagged, never read as zero, and a price outage shows as n/a.
    • Net (avg) is the book's time-weighted net exposure over its session closes. The tooltip adds "now". A book that is 69% net short today may have been net long on average, and the member page says both.

    A seat whose book has never held a priced position (the Decoder) reads UNRANKED and takes no rank (R33). The Decoder's row also says why, as NO BOOK with the reason.

    What the leaderboard is not: a record of skill (tested 2026-09-28). The owner asked whether the Executive should lean on the seats that lead the League, since leaders seem to run in seasons: Graham early, Black Swan now. A backtest tested that on the League's own record, and verifiers checked each result:
    • Form does not persist. A seat's past results did not predict its next ones on any basis, lookback or horizon: 0 of 284 tests. The early leaders were among September's worst.
    • The top seat is within luck. Black Swan's lead is stock selection, not its short bet. Even so, the best of 15 seats picking at random from the same slate beats it about 90% of the time.
    • Following the leaders lost money. Copying the top three seats' trades did worse than copying everyone. Weighting the room's grades by League record did no better than random weights.
    The leaderboard is a scoreboard of paper books. The courts ruled the same way independently (2026-09-15 and 2026-09-18, rulings 9, and R33): the chair never weights a seat by its equity rank. The idea is being tested forward as a shadow rather than dropped.

    The League-weight shadow test#

    Every morning from 2026-09-29, the desk freezes each seat's weight and prints a League-weighted median beside the real one. It is never shipped. The weight is rank-linear from 0.5 to 1.5, on the seat's clean hedged P&L over the five settled sessions before the run. A forward test registered on 2026-09-28 (commit a897090, before any eligible packet froze) scores the weighted vector against the real one on the 40-name slate as each run's five sessions settle.

    • Futility at 20 runs: if the weighted vector is doing no better than chance, the test stops there.
    • Decision at 40 runs, about mid-December. The idea becomes eligible for an owner ruling only if all three hold:
      • it beats weights shuffled at random across seats (p < 0.05);
      • a seat's trailing score predicts its next results;
      • the gain survives removing each name's own momentum.

    Courts see only RUNNING n=k, never the running score. The chair's prompt carries nothing from it. scripts/boardroom/league_weight_test.py status prints the state.

    The Decoder: NO BOOK, and its shadow book#

    The Decoder's row reads NO BOOK, followed by the reason in plain words. The League trades only a filed bull or bear stance. The Decoder files one only when its direction test passes, which needs two things:

    • its regime dial clears;
    • its held-out direction calls beat a naive rule by two paired standard errors.

    On runs 43–50 that happened on 0 of 320 slate reads, so the Decoder filed neutral on every line. Its only numbers are reach grades (G_OPTION), and a reach grade carries no stance (R84). This is the seat working as designed, not a bug.

    The owner ruled on 2026-10-06 that the Decoder gets a shadow book with no money and no rank. It is printed under the League table, in a group headed Shadow books (no money, unranked):

    • The bar. A call needs walk_forward.beats_naive_by_se of at least 1.42. There is no regime-dial requirement. That bar fires on 5 of 120 pure-noise tapes and on 11 of 120 tapes whose volatility clusters (re-measured 2026-09-29). On the real slate it passed 17 of 320 reads, about the rate chance gives. That is why the book holds no money.
    • The side is the sign of the read's own next-session edge, which is what the test scored. It is not the listed direction.
    • The slate is all 40 names when the session's packet is on disk, and the run's leads otherwise. Each date has one book: when a morning is rebuilt, the book that stood (the last one written) replaces the earlier build, with its own entry rule.
    • Recording. Each morning's run records its calls as the League's books open. If that record fails, the next mark records it late, with the same calls, entry and freeze time. Recording starts on 2026-10-07. A build deleted under an R32 tombstone has its rows removed with decoder_shadow_test.py forget --run N.
    • Fills and exits follow the League's own rule. A book written after 09:30 ET enters at the next session's open. Every call exits at the close of the run bar plus five. There are no midday or Bailiff exits, only settled bars are used, and each call is hedged against the S&P 500. P&L is quoted on $10,000 a call so it reads beside the clean column; no money is involved.
    • The reach ledger scores every reach grade other than 50 two-sided. Did the stock's daily high or low cover the break-even distance before expiry, upward or downward? A reach grade claims the size of a move, not its direction. A call whose stock reached that distance on the downside therefore counts as a touch.

    The graduation rule is pre-registered once, from a clean commit, by scripts/boardroom/decoder_shadow_test.py register, the same way as the League-weight test. Two limits apply to the count:

    • calls from runs whose packet froze before the registration never count;
    • holds on the same ticker that overlap count once.

    The decision is taken at 40 counted, settled calls, on those 40 only. The shadow is KEEP-ELIGIBLE only if both of these hold:

    • its SPY-hedged wins beat a coin flip, one-sided binomial p < 0.05 (26 or more wins of 40);
    • its summed hedged P&L is above zero.

    Otherwise it is NOT ELIGIBLE. KEEP-ELIGIBLE only makes the shadow eligible for an owner ruling; it never graduates by itself. The shadow never writes to the League's ledger (paper_positions, paper_equity), never enters the Pyramid, and never reaches any seat's or court's prompt.

    Replayed on runs 43–50, the shadow would have held 17 calls, 14 of them settled: +$4,329, or +$4,807 hedged, with 9 of the 14 winning. Those calls covered six names, and four overlapping FICO calls supplied most of the gain. The replay is not recorded and not eligible: its outcomes were known when the rule was written.

    Click a name: the trade history#

    Every name in the leaderboard is a link to that account's whole trade history. It opens #/member/<key>/paper — the member workspace with the Trade history tab already selected, so the League answers "what has this seat actually done" in one click rather than landing you on a dossier to hunt through. The Bot is a link too: it has no persona page, so its workspace renders book-only — the ledger, and nothing that would be blank.

    The ledger is one table of every position the account has opened, newest first, open and closed together. Splitting them answered "what does it hold" and "what did it close" but never "what has it done", which is the question the League sends you here to ask. Above it, six stat tiles: equity, realized P&L across closed trades, unrealized P&L across open ones, trades closed, win rate, and open now. Then the equity curve, then filter pills — All · Open · Closed — and the table itself.

    Columns: opened, ticker (linking to its chart), side, quantity, entry, exit or mark, closed date, P&L in dollars, return %, and why it closed. Open rows are tinted, carry an OPEN badge, and are marked at the latest quote — the server batches one quote call per page load and attaches mark, unrealized and unrealized_pct to each open row. A quote that does not arrive leaves those cells empty rather than falling back to the entry price: a position held at its own entry shows a P&L of exactly zero, which is a lie that looks like data. Closed rows carry the seat's own sentence for the exit — the midday closes read in the persona's voice ("INTU -5.72% — stop paying vig on a bet with no edge left"), tagged MIDDAY; a position that simply reached its five-day term reads held to term. Opened, Ticker, P&L and Return are sortable.

    The tab is part of the route, so #/member/graham/paper, /journal or /history can be linked, reloaded and pasted to someone else; switching tabs rewrites the URL with replaceState rather than re-navigating, so the page does not tear down and refetch to show a tab it has already loaded.

    Against the index#

    A paper account exists to answer a question that "did it make money" does not: did picking names beat buying the market? On a falling tape those have opposite answers, and this league has already produced the case — on 2026-08-26, eleven of sixteen accounts sat below their $100,000 start while the S&P 500 was down 1.32% over the same stretch, so eight of them were ahead of the index despite being down in absolute terms.

    So every Trade history carries an Against the S&P 500 block above the curve, and the curve itself carries the benchmark as a dashed second line. Three figures: this book's percentage change and its equity, SPY's percentage change and what the same money would be worth, and the difference in percentage points with a plain-language verdict — ahead of the index, behind the index, or level with the index. The header states the window it was measured over in sessions and dates, because that window is not the same for every seat.

    How it is built, and what it refuses to claim#

    The line starts where the money did, which is not always the first snapshot. A seat with no positions is seeded one flat row at the league's start equity, and for fourteen of the sixteen accounts that seed is the first snapshot — anchor there and both sides begin at $100,000 on the same close. The Glazier is the exception: its first mark reads $100,548.50, because it already held three positions when the marker first ran on it. Anchoring on that mark does two wrong things at once — it rebases the index $548.50 above the seed, and it quietly deletes the account's most profitable day from the account's own return. Under it the Glazier reported −0.61% and read behind the index, while its own Realized and Unrealized tiles, six inches up the same page, added to −0.06%. That seat is anchored one session earlier instead, at the league's start equity against the previous SPY close, where its money actually began — and it reads −0.1% against the index's −0.2%, ahead.

    On the member's own dates. There are eight distinct snapshot-date signatures across the sixteen accounts and three different start dates — 2026-08-14 for most, 2026-08-19 for the Glazier, 2026-08-25 for the Herald, who was seated that day. The benchmark is built per member on that member's own dates and never on a shared axis, and the chart aligns the two lines by date rather than by array position. A snapshot on a weekday holiday, which the mon-to-fri marker will eventually write, inherits the previous close rather than dropping out.

    Price return on both sides. Closes come from the league's own fetch — auto_adjust=False, the same raw prices the positions are marked at — rather than from the charting module, which is dividend-adjusted and would quietly disagree with the book after SPY's next ex-dividend date. Neither side collects dividends, so the comparison is like for like, and the note under the block says so rather than leaving you to assume total return.

    It says which way the book was leaning. "Ahead of a falling index" reads as stock-picking skill until you know the book was short it — and the two seats with the largest edges on 2026-08-26 were the two most short: Graham net short 60% of equity, the Herald short 30% with three positions and nothing long. So the note states net exposure in words before it states anything else.

    It says when the money was not at work. A seat that sat in cash through a falling tape can show up "ahead of the index" on days it had taken no position at all. The Skeptic's first snapshot is 2026-08-14 and its first trade is 2026-08-24: five sessions of that window compare cash with the index. When the idle stretch runs to two sessions or more, the note says so in words. Entries fill at the open, so the day a book first trades counts as invested, not idle — which is why the ordinary account, seeded flat at one close and buying at the next open, computes to zero idle sessions rather than one.

    It states its own sample size. The header reads "7 marks over 9 sessions" rather than a single number, because those are different quantities and the gap between them matters: the Skeptic's comparison spans nine sessions but rests on four marks. The dashed line is the index sampled on the account's snapshot dates, not the index's own path.

    What it does not print. No annualized figure and no Sharpe: snapshot spacing is uneven — gaps run from one to six trading days — and the Herald's two sessions of history would annualize to something absurd. No cross-member alpha table either, because ranking a seat with two marks against one with nine treats them as the same measurement. A member with fewer than two marks gets no comparison and is told which; a window reaching back past the fetched index history is clamped to the bars that exist and says so; and a genuine quote failure says that, rather than drawing nothing and letting an absent line read as a flat market.

    The Bot#

    The Bot has no persona and no opinions. It is the room's control group: the Executive's signed book, executed mechanically — the first five of its printed rank order, whatever the grade, same direction as ranked, same 10 % sizing, same five-day hold. When a philosophy's book beats The Bot over a window, that seat's convictions added something the Executive's synthesis did not; when The Bot leads, the room's own ranking was the better trade. It is highlighted in the table so the comparison is never more than one glance away.

    Re-keyed to rank (the owner, 2026-10-07). Until then the Bot took the top five by final grade, and only grades of 60 or better. Since the 2026-09-11 court the share column ships the median of the seats that filed, and since 2026-09-28 the option column ships the room's median (R79), capped at 55. So the grades sit in the 50s (why), and the 60 line left the Bot almost silent: one entry, META on 2026-09-24, after its 2026-09-10 book. It now trades the first five of the printed rank order, whatever the grade. Since R81 (the 2026-09-25 court) that order is an unshipped shadow: the share column ships flat, and the morning memo names no top five as the book's selection. So the Bot scores that order as a book; it does not follow a pick the book made. Nor is it a claim of edge: the 2026-Q3 backtest found the grades do not rank returns. The rule applies from the first book opened after the ruling. A run's books open once and are never rewritten, so run 51 and every earlier book keep what they opened, and no Bot position was backfilled: the Bot's quiet weeks stay on its curve as they happened. The Spotlight and the staged-order drafts keep their own 60 line: the ruling named only the Bot.

    The League and the Fund#

    Round 27 added a second paper engine, The Fund, and the two are deliberately not merged: they answer different questions. The League asks which philosophy makes money, so it needs seventeen books and rules crude enough that every seat is scored on the same yardstick. The Fund asks what the board's shipped book is worth held as one portfolio, so it needs one book and one fixed rule for holding it: since 2026-09-28, the book rule, which replaced the grade line, each lead's own stop and target, and the allocation model.

    The Paper LeagueThe Fund
    Booksseventeen — one per grading seat, plus the Skeptic and The Botone
    What gets ineach seat's own top three by conviction; The Bot takes the first five of the book's printed rank order, whatever the grade (since 2026-10-07)every shipped share lead of the newest completed run, at the next session's open, on a name the fund does not already hold; no grade line since 2026-09-28
    Sizinga house constant: 10 % of the seat's equity per legequal weight within the day: each day's cohort gets the owner's allocation ÷ the five-session hold, split equally across its names, no name above 10 %; no model weights, no adds, no trims
    Exitsa flat five-trading-day hold, plus a midday close by the seat and a Bailiff killa fixed five-session hold: every lot leaves at the close of its fifth session (the fill session and four more); no stop, target, kill or grade-decay exit
    Optionstraded as the underlying; the League does not price contractsnot admitted unless fund_admit_options is on; even then the fund holds the contract itself, never the underlying, and leaves at the last session before expiry
    Rebalancingnone — a position is opened and then left alonenone since 2026-09-28 — a lot is sized once, when it is admitted; the daily job at 18:20 ET (idempotent per date) runs the exits and admits the day's cohort
    Taxnot modelleda tax lens: lot terms, estimated tax and a wash-sale flag — estimates, not tax advice; under the book rule there are no trims, so its after-tax hysteresis has nothing to veto
    The questionwhose philosophy was rightwhat the board's whole share book was worth, held equally for five sessions — the benchmark the 2026-Q3 backtest measured

    Both are paper by construction and neither has an execution path. Where they overlap they share code rather than agreeing by accident: the Fund fills through the same daily-bar history helpers this module uses, and both take the Bailiff's rule that an intraday touch never closes anything.

    Where the League feeds#

    • The Saturday Week in Review reads the League's equity deltas for the week; the Sunday Week Ahead carries the open paper positions into the prospectus.
    • The Midday Check-In packet is built from each member's open paper positions, so the League is the reason the 12:30 session has something concrete to decide.
    • Each member's workspace (PAPER BOOK tab, overview sparkline and stat chips) reads the same ledger.

    Honest limits#

    • Fills are the daily open and the daily close with no slippage, no commission, and fractional shares — a paper convention, not an execution model.
    • Option leads are traded as their underlying. A seat that was right about a contract's premium and wrong about the stock shows the stock's result.
    • Ten percent of equity per leg and a flat five-day hold are house constants. They are not optimized and the leaderboard does not reward timing beyond the midday close.
    • On 21 to 22 runs the League's rank order cannot be told apart from luck. The clean, hedged column removes the League's own conventions, but not chance.
    • Window P&L is measured on calendar days, so a 1W window over a holiday week compares four sessions, not five.
    • The League is evidence about the board, not about you. It never trades your money and cannot: the only code that submits a real order lives behind a human click on the Broker page, one order per click, and the League does not call it.

    API#

    GET /api/paper/league
    every seat: equity (as booked), P&L and % per window, open positions, win rate, last action, clean_pct / clean_hedged_pct / clean_n / clean_unpriced, net exposure now and time-weighted, book_opened; The Bot flagged. Beside the list: no_book (the NO BOOK reason, keyed by seat) and shadow_books (no money, no rank)
    GET /api/paper/shadow/decoder
    the Decoder's whole shadow book: every call, the reach ledger, the pre-registered test's state and the NO BOOK reason
    decoder_shadow_runs · decoder_shadow_calls · decoder_reach_calls
    the shadow's own tables, one call per (run, ticker); the book, its marks and the test read one run per date, the latest-written completed one, so a rebuilt book replaces the one it rebuilt; never paper_positions
    GET /api/paper/league/history?window=
    per-member equity series for the sparklines, capped to a readable length
    GET /api/paper/member/{key}
    equity curve, open positions, closed-trade log with exit reason and kind, window stats
    paper_start_equity
    setting, default 100000
    paper_positions · paper_equity
    the ledger and the daily snapshots; paper_equity is UNIQUE(member, equity_date)
